full.text: An ecosystem is made of biotic components (producers, consumers, decomposers) and abiotic components (light, temperature, water, soil, minerals).
The position of an organism in a food chain, such as producer or primary consumer.
Energy enters as sunlight, is fixed by producers in photosynthesis and passes along food chains. At each step much energy is lost as heat in respiration, in faeces and in uneaten parts.

items: Only about 10% of the energy at one trophic level is passed to the next
This limits food chains to usually four or five levels
Energy flows in one direction; nutrients are recycled

full.text: Elements such as carbon and nitrogen cycle between living organisms and the environment.

items: Photosynthesis removes CO2 from the air
Respiration, decomposition and combustion return CO2
Carbon is stored in fossil fuels and carbonate rocks
Nitrogen fixation: N2 to ammonia by bacteria such as *Rhizobium* in root nodules, and by lightning
Nitrification: ammonium to nitrite (*Nitrosomonas*) to nitrate (*Nitrobacter*)
Denitrification: nitrate back to N2 by denitrifying bacteria in waterlogged soils
Ammonification: decomposers turn proteins and urea into ammonium

written.stem: Explain why food chains rarely have more than five trophic levels.
written.model_answer: Only about 10% of energy passes from one level to the next. Energy is lost as heat in respiration, in faeces and urine, and in parts not eaten. After a few levels too little energy remains to support another population.

points.text: Too little energy for higher levels

written.stem: Describe the roles of bacteria in the nitrogen cycle.
written.model_answer: Nitrogen-fixing bacteria such as Rhizobium convert N2 into ammonia. Decomposers convert proteins and urea into ammonium (ammonification). Nitrosomonas oxidises ammonium to nitrite and Nitrobacter oxidises nitrite to nitrate (nitrification). Denitrifying bacteria convert nitrate to N2.

written.stem: List four threats to biodiversity and give an example of one.
written.model_answer: Habitat loss, overexploitation, invasive alien species, pollution and climate change threaten biodiversity. For example, deforestation destroys the habitat of forest species.

points.text: Pollution or climate change with example

written.stem: Explain how excess fertiliser can cause eutrophication of a lake.
written.model_answer: Nitrates and phosphates wash into the lake and cause rapid growth of algae (algal bloom). Algae block light and plants below die. Bacteria decompose the dead material and use up oxygen, so fish and other animals die.

written.stem: Describe the carbon cycle and explain how human activities affect it.
written.model_answer: Carbon dioxide is fixed by producers in photosynthesis and passed along food chains. Respiration by all organisms and decomposition return CO2 to the air. Some carbon is stored long term in fossil fuels and limestone. Burning fossil fuels and deforestation add CO2 faster than it is removed, increasing the greenhouse effect and causing global warming.

written.stem: Discuss in situ and ex situ methods of conserving biodiversity.
written.model_answer: In situ conservation protects species in their natural habitats, for example national parks, forest reserves and sanctuaries; it keeps ecosystems and interactions intact. Ex situ conservation keeps species outside their habitats, for example zoos, botanical gardens, seed banks and captive breeding; it protects species at high risk and can reintroduce them. Laws, education and sustainable use support both.

points.text: In situ examples: national park / reserve
Ex situ examples: zoo / seed bank / botanical garden

ask.question: Why is energy lost between trophic levels?
ask.answer: At each trophic level energy is lost as heat from respiration, in faeces and urine, and in parts that are not eaten. Only about 10% is passed on to the next level.

sources.title: A/L Biology syllabus (2025), topic 8.1: Ecosystem structure and energy flow

ask.question: What is nitrogen fixation?
ask.answer: Nitrogen fixation is the conversion of nitrogen gas into ammonia or other usable compounds. It is done by bacteria such as Rhizobium in legume root nodules, by free-living bacteria, by lightning and by the industrial Haber process.

sources.title: A/L Biology syllabus (2025), topic 8.2: Biogeochemical cycles

ask.question: What are the threats to biodiversity?
ask.answer: The main threats are habitat loss and fragmentation, overexploitation, invasive alien species, pollution and climate change.

sources.title: A/L Biology syllabus (2025), topic 8.6: Biodiversity and its threats

ask.question: What causes eutrophication?
ask.answer: Excess nitrates and phosphates, often from fertilisers or sewage, cause algal blooms. When the algae die, bacteria decompose them and use up the oxygen, so fish and other animals die.

sources.title: A/L Biology syllabus (2025), topic 8.7: Global environmental problems

ask.question: What is the difference between in situ and ex situ conservation?
ask.answer: In situ conservation protects species in their natural habitats, such as national parks. Ex situ conservation protects them outside their habitats, such as in zoos, botanical gardens and seed banks.

sources.title: A/L Biology syllabus (2025), topic 8.8: Conservation of biodiversity
